clinicalPearls: Caused by obstruction of the superior vena cava, either extrinsic compression or invasion by tumour or intraluminal thrombosis
Malignancy is the leading cause, particularly bronchogenic carcinoma (small-cell and squamous) and non-Hodgkin lymphoma
Thrombotic causes are increasingly common with indwelling central venous catheters and pacemaker leads
Presents with facial and neck swelling and plethora, distended neck and chest wall veins, arm swelling, headache, and dyspnoea, typically worse on bending forward or lying flat
Pemberton's sign (facial congestion on raising the arms) supports the diagnosis
Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest defines the level and cause of obstruction and guides biopsy; a tissue diagnosis is important because management depends on tumour type

Management is directed at the cause, treating the underlying malignancy (chemotherapy or radiotherapy) or thrombus (anticoagulation), with endovascular stenting for prompt symptom relief in severe or refractory cases
reference.pathophysiology: Superior vena cava syndrome results from obstruction to venous return through the SVC to the right atrium. Most cases are due to malignant mediastinal disease, commonly lung cancer or lymphoma, that compresses or invades the thin-walled, low-pressure SVC; thrombosis, frequently related to intravascular devices, is a growing non-malignant cause. Obstruction raises venous pressure in the head, neck, and upper limbs, producing oedema, venous distension, and the recruitment of collateral chest wall veins. The severity of symptoms depends on how rapidly the obstruction develops and whether collaterals have had time to form, with airway and cerebral oedema being the most dangerous consequences.
additionalDifferentials: Mediastinal fibrosis (for example fibrosing mediastinitis or post-radiation)
Nephrotic syndrome or other causes of facial oedema
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT of the chest to define the level, extent, and cause
Tissue diagnosis (sputum cytology, bronchoscopy, or biopsy of a nodal or mediastinal mass) to guide oncological treatment
CT or MR venography to map the obstruction and collaterals
Chest radiograph as an initial screen for mediastinal widening or mass
Venography at the time of stenting
Assessment for catheter- or lead-related thrombosis where relevant
redFlags: Stridor, laryngeal oedema, or respiratory compromise (an airway emergency)
Cerebral oedema with confusion, severe headache, or altered consciousness
Rapid onset of severe symptoms without collateral formation
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the underlying cause; malignant SVC syndrome reflects the prognosis of the tumour, although stenting and oncological therapy give rapid symptom relief, whereas benign thrombotic causes generally respond well to anticoagulation and stenting.
pitfalls: Starting empirical radiotherapy before obtaining a tissue diagnosis in a stable patient, potentially obscuring histology
Overlooking a catheter- or lead-related thrombus as the cause
Failing to recognise airway or cerebral compromise requiring urgent intervention
Assuming all SVC obstruction is malignant
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
ESVS Clinical Practice Guidelines on Venous Disease
management: Obtain a tissue diagnosis before treatment wherever it is clinically safe, as management depends on the tumour type
Use endovascular stent placement for prompt relief of severe symptoms regardless of the underlying histology
Treat the cause definitively, with chemotherapy for small-cell bronchogenic carcinoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma and radiotherapy for radiosensitive tumours
Manage catheter- or lead-related thrombotic obstruction with anticoagulation and device removal where appropriate
Give supportive care with head-of-bed elevation, oxygen and corticosteroids where there is airway or cerebral oedema
Escalate urgently for airway protection when stridor or laryngeal oedema develops
Refer to a multidisciplinary oncology team to guide tumour-directed treatment
